narrative:
The model predicts you have an 11% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this prediction were your number of past class failures, your weekly study time, and who acts as your guardian. Surprisingly, the strongest influence actually worked in your favor: having zero past failures is identical to the average among students who passed and pushed the model toward expecting you to succeed. Your choice of guardian also leaned slightly toward passing. However, your weekly study time of only 5–10 hours worked against you. Most students who passed spent either 2–5 hours or less than 2 hours per week; your higher study time placed you in a smaller group where the model sees less evidence of success.

Because the positive influences were not strong enough to outweigh the effect of your study habits, the model concluded you are at some risk of failing. To improve, you should focus on making your study time more consistent and effective rather than simply increasing the hours. Reviewing past material regularly, seeking help early when you feel stuck, and creating a structured weekly plan could turn your current study routine into a real advantage and help you comfortably pass next year.
